one_line_idea: Test-time augmentation ensembling for semantic segmentation follows a saturating logarithmic gain law whose slope is fully determined by the measured pairwise error decorrelation of the augmentation family, making the whole compute-quality curve predictable from two members.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Practitioners pick TTA ensemble sizes (number of scales/flips/crops averaged at inference) by habit; there is no accepted functional form for how dense-prediction quality grows with TTA member count.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Gain over single-pass inference fits a + b*log(N) with early saturation, and the coefficient b is a linear function of the mean pairwise error correlation among members, because TTA averaging is variance reduction over a fixed shared-bias floor.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across at least 3 augmentation families (scales, flips, photometric jitter) on Cityscapes, the log-law fit will achieve R^2 >= 0.9 on mIoU-vs-N curves and Spearman correlation between fitted slope b and measured pairwise error decorrelation will be >= 0.6; kill the idea if R^2 < 0.75 for 2 of 3 families or if the slope-decorrelation correlation is < 0.3.
why_important: A validated scaling law turns TTA budgeting from folklore into arithmetic: teams could compute the marginal mIoU per extra forward pass before buying it, and the shared-bias floor quantifies what TTA can never fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] TTA is ubiquitous but treated as a bag of tricks; a pre-registered functional-form test with a decorrelation-based slope model for dense prediction appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run SegFormer-B2 on Cityscapes val with TTA ensembles of N=1..16 drawn from three augmentation families, fit mIoU(N) curves, measure pairwise pixel-error correlations among members, and test the log-law fit and slope-decorrelation relation.
main_risk: Augmentation families interact with the architecture (e.g., scale TTA on a multi-scale backbone), producing family-specific curve shapes that defeat a single functional form.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More TTA is monotonically better with diminishing returns, and the exact curve is model-specific trivia not worth modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: TTA gains may be dominated by a few images with resolution-sensitive content, making dataset-level curves an average of bimodal per-image behavior that no smooth law captures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public SegFormer-B2 checkpoint on Cityscapes val (500 images), 16 augmented passes per family: about 6 GPU-hours total on one consumer GPU; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: Dense-prediction quality as a function of inference resolution follows a power law that breaks at the training resolution, and the break location is set by the positional-embedding interpolation scheme for ViT-based models but is absent in convolutional pyramids.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Inference resolution is the single largest test-time compute knob for dense models, yet papers report one or two resolutions and no community-agreed curve shape exists for quality versus inference resolution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Below training resolution, quality rises as a task-specific power law in pixel count; above it, ViT models plateau or degrade at a break point governed by how positional embeddings are interpolated, while fully convolutional models extend the power law further because their priors are resolution-covariant.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On ADE20K and Cityscapes, evaluating at 8 resolutions from 0.25x to 2x training resolution, a segmented power-law fit will locate a break within 15% of training resolution for ViT-based DPT/ViT-Adapter models but no detectable break (slope change < 30%) for SegFormer/DeepLabv3+ style pyramids; kill the idea if conv models break at the same place or ViT breaks are absent.
why_important: If the break is an embedding-interpolation artifact rather than a representation limit, cheap test-time fixes (better interpolation) unlock resolution scaling without retraining, and compute planning can use closed-form curves.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution sensitivity of ViTs is known qualitatively; a pre-registered segmented power-law comparison across architecture families with a break-location hypothesis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 4 public checkpoints (DPT, ViT-Adapter, SegFormer-B2, DeepLabv3+/ResNet-101) at 8 inference resolutions on ADE20K and Cityscapes val, fit segmented power laws per model, and compare break locations and slopes across families.
main_risk: Sliding-window evaluation protocols confound resolution with window tiling, so the curve may measure the eval harness rather than the model; whole-image inference is needed where memory allows.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher inference resolution helps until memory runs out, and how it helps is treated as model-specific tuning trivia.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Break points may be governed by learned object-scale priors in the data rather than positional-embedding mechanics, which would put conv and ViT models on the same footing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Four public checkpoints, 8 resolutions, ADE20K val (2000 images) and Cityscapes val (500): roughly 8 GPU-hours on one 24GB GPU; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: The exchange rate between train-time and test-time compute for object detection decays with model scale: test-time compute (TTA, multi-scale) recovers a large fraction of the gap to the next-larger model for small detectors but almost none for large ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Teams routinely choose between deploying a larger detector and adding inference-time enhancements to a smaller one, but there is no measured iso-accuracy map between the two compute types.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Small models' errors are dominated by input-representation noise that averaging fixes, while large models' residual errors are systematic (rare semantics, annotation-independent perceptual limits), so the AP fraction of the size-gap recoverable by test-time compute shrinks monotonically with scale.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO val with YOLOv8-n/s/m/l/x, full TTA plus multi-scale inference at matched extra FLOPs will recover >= 45% of the AP gap from n to s, but <= 15% of the gap from l to x; kill the idea if the recovered fraction is flat across scale (within 10 points) or increases with scale.
why_important: A decaying exchange rate is a deployment law: it tells practitioners at which model scale test-time compute stops substituting for parameters, and it constrains claims that inference-time scaling is a general alternative to model scaling in perception.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Inference-time compute scaling is heavily studied for language models; an iso-accuracy exchange-rate measurement across a detector size ladder appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate the YOLOv8 size ladder on COCO val with and without a fixed TTA/multi-scale protocol, compute per-pair gap recovery fractions, and plot recovered fraction versus model scale.
main_risk: TTA protocols interact with NMS settings differently per scale, so the protocol must re-tune fusion per model, otherwise the measured decay could be a fusion artifact.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] TTA gives roughly a constant AP bump (~1 point) regardless of model size, so the choice is a latency question, not a scaling question.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large models may be undertrained at high resolutions where TTA operates, in which case test-time compute could recover more, not less, of the gap at scale.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Five public YOLOv8 checkpoints (Ultralytics) on COCO val2017 with and without TTA: about 5 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: Sample-count scaling for stochastic dense predictors (diffusion-based depth like Marigold) hits a floor by roughly 10 samples that is set by shared mode bias, not residual variance, so ensembling more samples cannot close the gap to deterministic experts.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Diffusion-based dense predictors are ensembled over multiple noise seeds at inference and papers report gains from averaging around 10 samples, but where the sample-count curve saturates and why is not characterized.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across seeds the predictor samples from a distribution concentrated around a biased mode; averaging removes seed variance quickly (inverse-power decay) but leaves a bias floor that is invariant to sample count and correlated across scenes.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On NYUv2, Marigold AbsRel will improve by < 1% relative when going from 10 to 50 averaged samples, and the residual error map at N=50 will correlate (pixelwise Pearson >= 0.7) with the N=10 residual map, evidencing a stable bias; kill the idea if accuracy keeps improving by >= 3% relative beyond N=10 or residuals decorrelate (r < 0.4).
why_important: It sets a hard ceiling on inference-compute scaling for the stochastic-predictor route to dense perception and redirects effort from more samples to bias correction, the actual binding constraint.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ensemble sizes are reported as hyperparameters in diffusion-for-depth papers; a bias-variance decomposition of the sample-count curve with pre-registered saturation thresholds appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run Marigold on NYUv2 with N in {1,2,5,10,20,50} seeds, fit the error-vs-N curve to a variance-decay-plus-floor model, and measure cross-N residual-map correlations against Depth Anything v2 as a deterministic reference.
main_risk: Aggregation method (median vs mean, alignment per sample) changes the curve; conclusions must be shown robust to the fusion rule.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More samples monotonically improve stochastic dense predictors and the choice of 10 is a compute compromise, not a structural ceiling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At higher sample counts, better aggregation (e.g., pixelwise mode-seeking) might unlock multimodal structure that plain averaging wastes, resuming the scaling curve.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Marigold public checkpoint on NYUv2 test (654 images) at 6 sample counts: about 10 GPU-hours on one GPU; Depth Anything v2 reference adds 20 minutes; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: Sliding-window inference gains for segmentation saturate at window overlap around one-third because essentially all of the benefit is confined to a border band whose width equals the model's effective receptive-field deficit, making higher overlaps pure waste.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] High-resolution segmentation is evaluated with overlapping sliding windows and overlap ratio is a compute multiplier chosen by convention (often 1/2 or 2/3) with no mechanistic justification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Window predictions are only unreliable within a border band where context is truncated; once overlap covers that band, additional overlap re-computes already-reliable interior pixels, so the quality-vs-overlap curve saturates exactly when overlap width exceeds the band width.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes with Mask2Former sliding-window inference, >= 80% of the mIoU gain from overlap 0 to overlap 2/3 will be attributable to pixels within 64 px of window borders, and quality at overlap 1/3 will be within 0.2 mIoU of overlap 2/3; kill the idea if interior pixels account for > 40% of the gain or if overlap 2/3 beats 1/3 by > 0.5 mIoU.
why_important: Halving sliding-window compute for free across every high-resolution deployment is immediately actionable, and the border-band framing gives a measurable definition of effective context deficit at test time.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Overlap ratios are copied between codebases; a spatial decomposition of where overlap gains live, with a receptive-field-based saturation prediction, appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate Mask2Former on Cityscapes val at overlaps {0, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3}, decompose per-pixel gains by distance to window border, and compare the saturation overlap against the measured border-band width.
main_risk: Fusion rules (averaging logits in overlapped zones) may themselves add an ensembling gain in interiors, mixing two mechanisms; a border-masked fusion control separates them.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More window overlap is safer and the cost is accepted as the price of high-resolution inference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For models with very large effective receptive fields, even border bands may be reliable, making the curve flat everywhere and the band-width story unfalsifiable rather than wrong.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Mask2Former public checkpoint on Cityscapes val at 5 overlap settings: about 4 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: The area under a model's anytime inference curve (quality vs test-time compute across exits/scales) is a stable architecture-family property: rankings by anytime area transfer across datasets even when rankings by peak accuracy do not.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Models are compared at a single operating point (peak accuracy at full compute), yet deployments sweep compute budgets; there is no evidence on whether compute-quality curves are a stable model property or a per-dataset accident.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The shape of the anytime curve reflects architectural commitments (feature reuse, pyramid structure, exit-head cost) that are dataset-independent, so normalized anytime area ranks model families consistently across datasets.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For 6 public classification/detection backbones (ResNet-50, ConvNeXt-T, ViT-B, Swin-T, EfficientNet-B3, DeiT-S) each given the same multi-resolution anytime protocol, the cross-dataset Spearman correlation of anytime-area rankings across ImageNet, ImageNet-R and ObjectNet will be >= 0.7 while peak-accuracy rankings correlate <= 0.5; kill the idea if anytime-area rankings are no more stable than peak-accuracy rankings (difference < 0.1).
why_important: If anytime area is a portable property, model selection for compute-variable deployments can be done once on a proxy dataset, and papers should report curves rather than points.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anytime prediction is studied per-method; treating anytime area as a transferable model-family invariant with a pre-registered stability comparison appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a uniform anytime protocol (inference at 5 resolutions, cumulative best), compute anytime areas for 6 backbones on 3 public datasets, and compare rank stability of areas vs peaks.
main_risk: The anytime protocol choice (resolution sweep vs early exits) may itself favor certain families, so two independent protocols must agree before claiming a family property.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Model comparisons at peak compute are representative, and compute-quality curves are implementation details.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Anytime area may be dominated by low-compute behavior that is as dataset-dependent as peak accuracy, destroying the claimed stability.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Six public timm checkpoints evaluated at 5 resolutions on ImageNet-val, ImageNet-R and ObjectNet subsets (10k images each): about 6 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: Multi-scale TTA gains reported for semantic segmentation are mostly boundary-pixel effects: under boundary-tolerant evaluation the claimed robustness gains shrink dramatically, revealing TTA as spatial averaging rather than evidence integration.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers report mIoU gains of 0.5-1.5 points from multi-scale TTA and often narrate them as robustness improvements; mIoU mixes boundary localization and region classification, so the source of the gain is unidentified.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale averaging mainly smooths boundary jitter between scales; interior-region label decisions rarely flip, so TTA buys boundary polish, not better scene understanding.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On ADE20K and Cityscapes with SegFormer-B5 and Mask2Former, >= 70% of the multi-scale TTA mIoU gain will disappear when evaluation excludes a 12 px band around ground-truth boundaries, and interior-region flips will affect < 1% of pixels; kill the idea if interior-only gains retain >= 50% of the headline gain on either dataset.
why_important: It reclassifies a universally used trick: if TTA is boundary polish, robustness claims built on TTA deltas are miscategorized, and cheap boundary-refinement heads could replace 3-5x inference cost.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boundary-vs-interior decompositions exist for architecture comparisons, but a pre-registered decomposition of TTA gains specifically appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two public checkpoints with and without standard multi-scale+flip TTA on ADE20K/Cityscapes val, recompute metrics with boundary bands excluded at 4/8/12 px, and count interior label flips.
main_risk: Boundary-band exclusion also removes genuinely hard thin objects (poles, signs), potentially hiding real TTA gains on thin structures; a thin-object class breakdown controls this.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multi-scale TTA integrates complementary evidence across scales and its gains reflect genuinely better predictions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On datasets with large scale variance (ADE20K), scale TTA may genuinely rescue misclassified small objects, which the interior-flip count would reveal as > 1%.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two public checkpoints (SegFormer-B5, Mask2Former) on Cityscapes val and ADE20K val with/without TTA plus band-masked scoring: about 6 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: A two-tier inference policy - most images at low resolution, a minority flagged by cheap two-scale disagreement re-run at high resolution - beats uniform mid-resolution inference at matched dataset-level FLOPs for object detection.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Deployed detectors run every image at the same resolution although per-image difficulty varies enormously, wasting compute on easy images and starving hard ones.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Disagreement between predictions at two cheap scales is a label-free flag for resolution-sensitive images; routing only flagged images to high resolution converts wasted uniform compute into targeted compute where it changes answers.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO val with RT-DETR-R50, a policy running all images at 480 px and the flagged 25% also at 960 px will beat uniform 640 px inference by >= 1.0 mAP at equal or lower total FLOPs; kill the idea if the gain is < 0.3 mAP or the required flag rate to reach parity exceeds 60%.
why_important: It demonstrates that dataset-level inference budgets, not per-image settings, are the right optimization unit for perception deployments, with immediate cost savings at fixed quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dynamic-resolution inference exists for classification; a matched-FLOPs two-tier routing policy driven by cross-scale disagreement for detection, with pre-registered thresholds, appears untested. Distinct from accepted W13-P1-L-025, which allocates agentic crops/samples in VLM loops; this is a single non-LLM detector routing its own resolution.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-image predictions at 480/640/960 px on COCO val with RT-DETR, define disagreement as unmatched-detection rate between 480 and 640 outputs, sweep the routing threshold, and compare mAP-vs-FLOPs frontiers against uniform policies.
main_risk: Disagreement flags may correlate with images that are hard at any resolution, in which case rerouting buys nothing; the frontier comparison exposes this directly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-image adaptive resolution is an engineering nicety with marginal value next to picking one good resolution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: COCO images are small and fairly uniform in difficulty structure; the policy may only pay off on higher-variance data, making the COCO test a false kill.
fastest_falsification_experiment: RT-DETR-R50 public checkpoint, COCO val2017 at three resolutions plus routing simulation done offline from cached predictions: about 4 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: Flip/rotation TTA gain is quantitatively the model's equivariance error cashed out at test time: per-class TTA gains track measured equivariance violations, and models trained with equivariance regularization gain almost nothing from group TTA.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Horizontal-flip TTA is near-universal in detection and segmentation pipelines, but why it helps some classes and models more than others has no accepted mechanistic account.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Group-averaging TTA implements at inference the invariance the model failed to learn; therefore the gain per class equals a function of the measured output discrepancy under the group action, and closing the discrepancy at training time (consistency regularization) removes the TTA gain.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO with YOLOv8-m, per-class flip-TTA AP gains will correlate with per-class flip-discrepancy (Spearman >= 0.5), and a flip-consistency-fine-tuned model will retain < 30% of its former TTA gain at unchanged base AP; kill the idea if the correlation is < 0.25 or the regularized model keeps > 60% of the TTA gain.
why_important: It converts TTA from ritual to diagnostic: measured equivariance error tells you the exact expected value of group TTA, and training-time consistency can permanently bank the gain, deleting a 2x inference cost.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Equivariance and TTA are separately mature topics; the identity claim - TTA gain equals deferred equivariance training, testable by regularize-then-remeasure - appears unstated. Distinct from off-master W13-P1-G-009, which critiques augmentation-consistency single-sample adaptation methods; this is a mechanism law for standard group-averaging TTA.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-class flip discrepancy and flip-TTA gain for a public YOLOv8-m on COCO val, then fine-tune 2 epochs with flip-consistency loss and remeasure both quantities.
main_risk: Consistency fine-tuning may slightly change base accuracy, confounding the retention measurement; matched-accuracy checkpoints control this.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Flip TTA is free insurance whose gains are idiosyncratic noise not worth modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: TTA may also average box-regression noise unrelated to symmetry, leaving a floor of gain that survives perfect equivariance and caps the correlation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: YOLOv8-m public checkpoint on COCO val for discrepancy/TTA measurement (2 GPU-hours) plus a 2-epoch consistency fine-tune (about 8 GPU-hours on one GPU); public data and model only.

one_line_idea: At matched inference FLOPs, multi-crop ensembling and single-pass high-resolution inference are not interchangeable: crops win on datasets with high object-scale variance, single-pass wins where long-range context matters, with a measurable dataset statistic locating the crossover.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cropping buys effective resolution at the cost of context truncation; its net value is positive exactly when the object-scale distribution has heavy small-object tails and negative when label decisions depend on scene-level context, so the object-scale variance of a dataset determines the winner.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 4 public detection/segmentation datasets ordered by object-scale variance (COCO, LVIS, Cityscapes, VisDrone), the crop-vs-single-pass advantage at matched FLOPs will switch sign monotonically with the scale-variance statistic, with VisDrone favoring crops by >= 2 AP and Cityscapes favoring single-pass by >= 0.5 mIoU; kill the idea if the ordering of advantages is uncorrelated with the statistic (Spearman < 0.4).
why_important: A validated selector removes a silent, compute-equivalent design choice that currently varies by community habit and confounds cross-paper comparisons of inference-time scaling claims.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Tiling folklore exists per domain; a cross-dataset matched-FLOPs comparison with a pre-registered dataset-statistic crossover appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For YOLOv8-l and SegFormer-B2, implement crop-ensemble and large-input protocols with equal FLOPs on the 4 datasets, compute the advantage per dataset, and regress against measured object-scale variance.

one_line_idea: Instances that remain unstable across the refinement stages of a cascade detector are the same instances that flip across ensemble members, revealing a single latent per-instance difficulty that both iteration and ensembling measure but neither fixes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Iterative refinement (cascade stages) and ensembling are both used to spend more inference compute per image, but whether they attack the same residual errors or complementary ones is unknown.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Both mechanisms reduce decision variance around a shared difficulty landscape; therefore instance-level instability under cascade stages and disagreement across ensemble seeds are strongly associated, and combining the two mechanisms is largely redundant.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With Cascade R-CNN on COCO val, instances whose class/box change materially between stages 2 and 3 will show >= 3x the ensemble-disagreement rate (across 3 seeds) of stage-stable instances, and adding ensembling on top of the cascade will recover < 35% of the AP gain that ensembling gives a single-stage baseline; kill the idea if the instability-disagreement association is < 1.5x or combined gains are additive (> 70% retained).
why_important: If iteration and ensembling are interchangeable probes of one difficulty axis, deployments should buy whichever is cheaper and papers should stop stacking both as if their gains compound. Distinct from accepted W13-P1-K-026, which claims recurrent flow refinement is replaceable by a single-pass architecture; this idea measures error-overlap between two test-time compute mechanisms on detection.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cascades and ensembles are compared as methods on leaderboards; an instance-level shared-difficulty association study between them appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run Cascade R-CNN (3 seeds available in MMDetection zoo or retrained cheaply) on COCO val, log per-instance stage trajectories and cross-seed disagreements, compute the association, and measure marginal ensemble AP on cascade vs Faster R-CNN.
main_risk: Matching instances across stages and members requires IoU-based bookkeeping whose thresholds could manufacture or hide the association; report sensitivity across matching IoUs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Refinement fixes localization and ensembling fixes classification variance, so their gains stack.

one_line_idea: Replacing greedy NMS with global hypothesis selection - solving the box-selection problem as an exact optimization over the score-overlap graph at test time - recovers substantial AP on crowded scenes from detectors that are already trained, no retraining required.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Greedy NMS makes irreversible local choices in score order; in crowded scenes an early suppression can delete a correct box that a globally optimal selection would keep, yet nearly all deployed detectors still decode greedily.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detector heads already emit enough correct candidate boxes in crowds; the binding loss is greedy selection, so casting selection as maximum-weight independent set on the overlap graph (solved exactly or near-exactly per image at test time) recovers recall that greedy decoding forfeits.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On CrowdHuman with a public Faster R-CNN baseline, exact/ILP selection over the same candidate set with tuned pairwise exclusion will beat best-tuned greedy NMS and Soft-NMS by >= 2.0 AP and >= 3.0 MR-2 improvement, while on COCO the gain will be <= 0.5 AP (crowding-specific mechanism); kill the idea if crowded-scene gain is < 0.8 AP over Soft-NMS or the candidate pool lacks the missing boxes (oracle-selection gain < 3 AP).
why_important: Decoding is pure test-time compute: a validated global-selection gain shows the standard detection pipeline leaves accuracy in the decoder, reframing NMS as a search problem with a measurable optimality gap.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Alternatives to NMS exist (Soft-NMS, learned NMS, set prediction); a pre-registered optimality-gap accounting between greedy and exact selection on modern crowded benchmarks appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Export raw candidates (pre-NMS) from a public CrowdHuman-trained Faster R-CNN, run greedy NMS, Soft-NMS, and an ILP/exact solver per image (small graphs after score thresholding), and compare AP/MR-2 plus oracle selection.
main_risk: Per-image ILP latency may be impractical at high candidate counts; the claim is about the optimality gap, but a practical variant (local search) must also be reported to matter.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] NMS is effectively solved plumbing; end-to-end set-prediction heads are the only serious alternative to greedy decoding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In heavy crowds the candidate pool may genuinely miss occluded instances (a representation failure, not a search failure), which the oracle-selection control would expose.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public CrowdHuman Faster R-CNN checkpoint (MMDetection), cached candidates on the 4370-image val set, CPU solver experiments: about 3 GPU-hours plus 10 CPU-hours; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: Beam width in autoregressive detectors saturates by width 4 because their residual errors are perceptual misclassifications, not sequence-decoding mistakes - test-time search cannot buy what the encoder never saw.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Autoregressive detection heads (Pix2Seq-style) expose language-model-like decoding knobs (beam width, sampling), but whether detection benefits from deeper decoding search the way text generation does is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In text, search fixes exposure and ordering errors; in detection, the token distribution is dominated by visual evidence, so alternative beams mostly reshuffle box order rather than discover new correct objects, and gains stop once the top few sequences are covered.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With a public Pix2Seq implementation on COCO val, going from greedy to beam 4 will add <= 0.5 AP, beam 16 will add <= 0.3 AP over beam 4, and >= 70% of residual false negatives at beam 16 will be objects absent from all beams (never generated), evidencing perceptual rather than search limits; kill the idea if beam 16 adds > 1.0 AP over beam 4 or most missed objects appear in some beam.
why_important: It cleanly separates two readings of test-time compute for structured perception - search over outputs vs better evidence - and warns against porting LLM inference-scaling intuitions to perception decoders.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pix2Seq reports mention nucleus sampling tricks; a beam-width scaling study with never-generated error accounting appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the public Pix2Seq checkpoint at beam widths {1,4,16} on COCO val, log all beam contents, classify false negatives into in-some-beam vs never-generated, and plot AP vs beam width.
main_risk: Sequence-length truncation and EOS handling differ across beam settings; decoding hyperparameters must be tuned per width to avoid strawman baselines.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Autoregressive heads should inherit LLM-style gains from better decoding search.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For small objects emitted late in sequences, beams may genuinely diverge and rescue misses, pushing beam-16 gains above threshold specifically on small-object AP.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public Pix2Seq (official repo) checkpoint on COCO val2017 at three beam widths: about 8 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: Emission order is a free test-time search variable for autoregressive detection: decoding under multiple object-emission orders and merging the results specifically rescues small objects that single-order decoding truncates away.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Sequence detectors emit objects in one learned order and stop at EOS; anything the order pushes late competes with termination, but decoding is run once with one order at test time.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Late-sequence positions systematically under-emit small/peripheral objects (truncation pressure); re-decoding under different order-inducing prompts (spatial raster variants, size-ascending vs descending) surfaces complementary object sets whose union recovers the truncated tail.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With a public Pix2Seq-style model on COCO val, merging detections from 4 order variants will raise small-object AP (APs) by >= 1.5 points over single-order decoding at matched total compute vs beam search of equal cost, and >= 60% of the newly recovered objects will come from late sequence positions of some variant; kill the idea if APs gain is < 0.5 or recovered objects are position-uniform.
why_important: It identifies output-ordering as a perception-specific search axis with no LLM analog and offers a training-free fix for a known small-object weakness of sequence detectors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Order sensitivity of sequence detectors is discussed at training time (label ordering); exploiting order diversity as test-time search appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Decode the public checkpoint under 4 emission-order conditions (achieved via coordinate-system remapping of the input/prompt tokens), merge with standard box fusion, and stratify gains by object size and sequence position.
main_risk: If the model was trained under one fixed order, alternative orders may be out-of-distribution and emit garbage, making the merge net-negative; per-variant AP must be reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Emission order is a training detail that decoding cannot usefully change after the fact.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Truncation may reflect score thresholds rather than order, in which case longer decoding budgets, not order diversity, would capture the same objects more cheaply.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public Pix2Seq checkpoint on COCO val2017, 4 decode variants plus fusion: about 10 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: Class-specific NMS radii can be searched on unlabeled target data at test time using a label-free stability objective (invariance of surviving-box counts under input jitter), beating global NMS settings without touching training or labels.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] One global NMS IoU threshold is applied across classes whose spatial statistics differ wildly (pedestrians overlap; stop signs do not), and per-class tuning is skipped because it needs labeled validation data per deployment domain.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The correct per-class suppression radius manifests as a stability signature: at the right radius, the set of surviving detections is invariant to small input perturbations, while over/under-suppression amplifies count churn, so stability search recovers near-oracle per-class thresholds label-free.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On LVIS val with YOLOv8-l, per-class NMS radii selected by jitter-stability on unlabeled images will recover >= 60% of the AP gain of oracle per-class radii (tuned on labels) over the global default, adding >= 0.7 box AP overall; kill the idea if recovery is < 25% or stability-selected radii are uncorrelated with oracle radii (Spearman < 0.3).
why_important: It demonstrates label-free test-time hyperparameter search for a decoder knob everyone hardcodes, with a mechanism (stability) that generalizes to other decoding parameters.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Adaptive NMS variants exist trained on labels; unlabeled-target stability search for per-class decoding parameters appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cache detections under 5 input jitters on LVIS val, sweep per-class radii, select by stability, and compare AP against global default and label-tuned oracle radii.
main_risk: Stability may prefer aggressive suppression (fewer boxes are trivially stabler); the objective needs a count-preservation term, which is part of the design being tested.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] NMS thresholds are set once per detector and generalize; per-class tuning is not worth the labeled-data cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For rare LVIS classes the jitter statistics are too sparse to estimate stability, potentially restricting the method to frequent classes only.
fastest_falsification_experiment: YOLOv8-l public checkpoint, LVIS v1 val cached inference under 5 jitters: about 8 GPU-hours on one GPU plus CPU search; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: Detection-ensemble fusion gains come overwhelmingly from coordinate averaging, not score averaging: fusing boxes with averaged geometry but single-member scores captures most of the Weighted-Box-Fusion improvement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Weighted Box Fusion and similar ensemble decoders average both geometry and scores of matched boxes, and their gains are reported as a lump sum with no attribution to the two channels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Localization noise across members is nearly independent and averages toward truth, while scores share bias; therefore geometry averaging is the active ingredient and score averaging is mostly inert.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO val fusing YOLOv8-l and RT-DETR-R50, geometry-only fusion (averaged coordinates, member-1 scores) will capture >= 70% of full WBF's AP gain over the best single member, while score-only fusion (member-1 boxes, averaged scores of matches) captures <= 30%; kill the idea if score-only fusion captures >= 50% or geometry-only under 40%.
why_important: Attribution changes ensemble engineering: if geometry is the channel that matters, cheap box-refinement heads or single-model geometric jitter-averaging could substitute for full multi-model ensembles at a fraction of the compute.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] WBF is widely used in competitions; a channel-ablated attribution of its gains appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cache detections from both public checkpoints on COCO val, implement full WBF plus the two ablated fusions with identical matching, and compare AP deltas, additionally stratifying by IoU threshold (AP50 vs AP75) to localize the geometric mechanism.
main_risk: The two members' score scales differ; score-only fusion must include per-member score normalization or its failure would be trivial.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Ensemble fusion works because averaging scores stabilizes evidence; geometry averaging is a minor smoothing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At AP50 (loose localization), score effects on the precision-recall ranking may dominate, reversing the attribution precisely where most practical metrics live.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two public checkpoints, cached COCO val2017 inference, CPU fusion ablations: about 3 GPU-hours plus 2 CPU-hours; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: A second decoding pass that re-scores below-threshold proposals conditioned on the accepted detections (co-occurrence and geometric-context energy, no language model) recovers occlusion-heavy recall that single-pass thresholding forfeits.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detector decoders make one pass of accept/reject decisions with a global score threshold; weak evidence for a partially occluded person next to a confidently detected bicycle is discarded even though accepted context makes it far more plausible.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection scores are context-blind at decode time; a cheap second pass that boosts rejected proposals consistent with accepted objects (learned co-occurrence priors and support relations estimated from training statistics) converts contextual plausibility into recall without hallucinating, because the boost is confined to proposals the detector itself generated.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On CrowdHuman and COCO-persons with a public Faster R-CNN, context re-scoring will add >= 1.5 AR@100 and >= 0.8 AP on occlusion-tagged subsets while changing full-set AP by > -0.2 (no net hallucination cost); kill the idea if occluded-subset gains are < 0.5 AR or full-set AP drops by > 0.5.
why_important: It spends a trivial amount of extra test-time compute exactly on the known weak spot of one-pass decoding (occlusion), and it isolates contextual reasoning as a decoder-level - not representation-level - deficit.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context rescoring existed in pre-deep-learning detection; a modern proposal-resurrection pass with pre-registered no-hallucination accounting on occlusion subsets appears untested on current detectors.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Export accepted and rejected proposals from the public checkpoint, estimate co-occurrence/geometry priors from COCO train annotations, implement the boost rule, and evaluate on occlusion-stratified val subsets.
main_risk: Context priors learned from training statistics may encode dataset-specific biases that inflate recall on benchmark scenes but not in the wild; cross-dataset replication (COCO to CrowdHuman) is included as a control.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Modern backbones already integrate context via attention, so decoder-level context passes are redundant.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If backbone attention has already priced context into the scores, resurrected proposals will be mostly true rejections and the no-hallucination margin will fail.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public MMDetection Faster R-CNN on COCO val2017 and CrowdHuman val with cached proposals plus CPU rescoring: about 5 GPU-hours plus 4 CPU-hours; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: Query count in DETR-family detectors is a test-time dial with a crowdedness-dependent sign: raising queries at inference improves crowded-scene recall but degrades sparse-scene precision, following a predictable operating-envelope shift.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] DETR-style models are trained with a fixed query budget (e.g., 100 or 300) and evaluated with the same budget; whether the query count can be usefully changed at inference, and what it trades, is folklore.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Queries act as slots competing through self-attention; adding slots at inference relaxes the competition (more candidates survive, helping crowds) but also weakens the learned slot-deduplication equilibrium (duplicate leakage, hurting sparse scenes), so the effect direction is governed by instance density.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With public DINO-DETR on COCO val, doubling inference queries will raise recall on images with > 15 instances by >= 2 points while lowering AP on images with < 4 instances by >= 0.5, and the per-image effect sign will be predicted by instance count with >= 65% accuracy; kill the idea if the model is insensitive to inference-time query count (all deltas < 0.3) or effects are density-independent.
why_important: A working density-conditioned query policy would give DETR deployments a free per-scene knob, and the slot-competition account would clarify what query training actually equilibrates.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Query-count ablations exist at training time; inference-time query-budget manipulation with a density-dependent sign prediction appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate DINO-DETR at {0.5x, 1x, 2x} inference query budgets (replicating/interpolating learned query embeddings) on COCO val, stratify AP/recall by instance count, and test the sign predictor.
main_risk: Naive query replication may be out-of-distribution for the decoder; embedding-space jitter or learned-query resampling variants must be tried before declaring insensitivity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Query count is a training architecture constant; changing it at inference either breaks the model or does nothing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The deduplication equilibrium may be robust to extra slots (attention just ignores them), producing the null result the kill condition anticipates.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public DINO-DETR checkpoint on COCO val2017 at three query budgets: about 4 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and model only.

one_line_idea: Multi-scale test-time inference for detectors is mostly a patch for scale-prior mismatch, not evidence integration: after per-scale score normalization and scale-aware box reweighting in single-scale inference, the residual multi-scale gain collapses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multi-scale testing reliably adds detection AP and is narrated as integrating complementary evidence across scales, at 3-5x inference cost.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detectors carry training-scale priors (anchor/stride statistics, size-conditioned score offsets); multi-scale testing largely re-aligns objects to the prior rather than adding information, so an explicit scale-conditioned score/box correction applied in one pass reproduces most of the gain.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO val with Faster R-CNN and YOLOX-l, a single-scale pass augmented with size-conditioned score correction (fit label-free from prediction statistics across two scales on unlabeled data) will retain >= 60% of the full multi-scale-TTA AP gain at 1.1x compute; kill the idea if retention is < 30% on both detectors or the correction damages base AP by > 0.3.
why_important: If most of the multi-scale gain is a correctable prior artifact, deployments save 3-5x compute, and reported multi-scale robustness narratives need re-attribution.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scale-mismatch analyses exist at training time (SNIP-style); a test-time correction that substitutes for multi-scale TTA with pre-registered retention thresholds appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit size-conditioned score/box corrections from unlabeled two-scale prediction discrepancies, apply in single-scale inference, and compare against full multi-scale TTA on COCO val for both detectors.
main_risk: The correction may effectively memorize COCO size statistics rather than fix a model prior, failing to transfer to other data; a LVIS transfer check is included.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multi-scale testing works because different scales see genuinely different evidence that must all be computed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For small objects near the resolution floor, upscaled passes may create truly new evidence (legible textures) that no score correction can synthesize, keeping retention below threshold.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two public checkpoints on COCO val2017 with cached two-scale statistics and CPU correction fitting: about 8 GPU-hours on one GPU; public data and models only.

one_line_idea: Instance segmentation quality improves when decoding is run as candidate-set search: generate redundant mask candidates from multiple proposal sources, then select a subset by maximizing an image-level coherence energy (non-overlap, boundary-image alignment, coverage) with local search at test time.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Instance pipelines produce candidate masks and select them greedily per candidate (score threshold + NMS); the resulting set often has overlaps, holes, and boundary disagreements that no per-candidate rule can fix because coherence is a set property.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large fraction of mask errors are selection errors: the right masks exist among candidates but greedy per-candidate acceptance picks an incoherent subset, so optimizing a set-level energy at test time recovers quality without new training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO instance val with Mask R-CNN plus FreeSOLO as complementary candidate sources, coherence-energy subset selection will beat score-threshold+NMS selection over the pooled candidates by >= 1.2 mask AP, and oracle subset selection will show >= 5 mask AP headroom confirming selection (not generation) as the bottleneck; kill the idea if the energy-based gain is < 0.4 mask AP or oracle headroom is < 2 AP.
why_important: It reframes instance decoding as combinatorial test-time search with a measurable optimality gap and gives a principled use for heterogeneous mask sources that are currently fused naively.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Set-energy selection over pooled multi-source mask candidates with pre-registered oracle-gap accounting appears distinct from both classic CRF post-processing and learned mask fusion.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pool candidates from the two public models on COCO val, define the coherence energy (pairwise overlap penalty, boundary-edge alignment, image coverage), run greedy+swap local search per image, and compare against threshold+NMS and oracle selection.
main_risk: Energy weights need tuning without labels; if performance is hypersensitive to weights, the method reduces to hidden supervised tuning - report sensitivity curves.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Post-hoc mask selection is solved by score thresholding; remaining errors require better mask heads, not better selection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Candidate pools may lack correct masks precisely for the hard instances (generation bottleneck), which the oracle-headroom control would reveal, killing the search framing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public Mask R-CNN and FreeSOLO checkpoints on COCO val2017 with cached candidates plus CPU local search: about 6 GPU-hours plus 8 CPU-hours; public data and models only.
